name: Ubuntu
summary: The most popular desktop Linux. Big community, easy to find help.
specs: Snap app store, plus deb packages
LTS release every 2 years, 5 years of updates
disadvantages: Snap apps can feel slow to start

name: Linux Mint
summary: Familiar Windows-like desktop. Calm, stable and polished.
advantages: Traditional menu layout, easy for Windows users
No Snap store forced on you
disadvantages: Cinnamon uses more RAM than Xfce

name: Zorin OS
summary: Made for people leaving Windows. Clean design, runs on old PCs.
specs: Pro layout pack paid, core is free
advantages: Very low hardware needs for the Lite edition
Simple installer with NVIDIA driver option
Polished look out of the box
disadvantages: Some layouts locked behind paid Pro
Upgrades between versions can be slow to arrive

name: elementary OS
summary: Beautiful, simple desktop inspired by macOS. Opinionated and tidy.
disadvantages: Less customisable than KDE or Cinnamon
requirements: Recent Intel i3 or comparable dual-core 64-bit CPU
Solid state drive with 15 GB free

name: Pop!_OS
summary: Developer and gaming friendly, from computer maker System76.
specs: COSMIC desktop project from System76; older releases use GNOME
advantages: Excellent NVIDIA support out of the box
Great for gaming and ML work
disadvantages: Desktop and features depend on the release you choose

name: Kubuntu
summary: Ubuntu with the KDE Plasma desktop. Pretty and very customisable.
disadvantages: KDE apps look different from GNOME ones

name: Xubuntu
summary: Ubuntu with the light Xfce desktop. Good balance of looks and speed.
advantages: Stable, rarely changes in surprising ways
disadvantages: Looks a little dated by default

name: Lubuntu
summary: The light Ubuntu flavour, using LXQt. Built for older hardware.
advantages: Runs well on old, low-RAM PCs
Easy access to all Ubuntu software
disadvantages: LXQt has fewer themes than KDE

name: Linux Lite
summary: Aimed squarely at Windows switchers with older PCs.
disadvantages: Based on LTS, so apps age

name: MX Linux
summary: Popular, practical Debian-based desktop with handy MX tools.
advantages: Good middle ground of light and pretty
disadvantages: Less polish than Mint or Zorin

name: Fedora Workstation
summary: Fresh, near-latest software on a clean GNOME desktop.
disadvantages: Needs a system upgrade about every year
Some media codecs need extra setup
requirements: 2 GB RAM plus memory for your apps

name: Debian
summary: The rock-solid base of Ubuntu and many others. Slow, steady, free.
specs: Choice of GNOME, KDE, Xfce and more
disadvantages: Installer plainer than Mint or Ubuntu
Check firmware and hardware support before installing
requirements: 1 GB RAM (2 GB recommended) with desktop

name: openSUSE Tumbleweed
summary: Tested rolling release. Always current, rarely breaks.
disadvantages: YaST can feel unusual to Ubuntu users

name: Manjaro
summary: Arch Linux made easier, with a friendly installer and tools.
advantages: Arch software freshness without the manual install
disadvantages: Holds packages back, so not pure Arch
Check release notes before major updates

name: EndeavourOS
summary: A friendly on-ramp to real Arch. Terminal-first but welcoming.
specs: Many desktop choices at install time
advantages: You learn how your system works
disadvantages: Not ideal as a very first distro

name: KDE neon
summary: Latest KDE Plasma on a stable Ubuntu LTS base.
advantages: First access to new KDE features
disadvantages: Non-KDE apps come from older LTS repos
Some rough edges in early KDE releases

name: Garuda Linux
summary: Gaming-focused Arch with snapshots, Zen kernel and bold themes.
specs: ZEN kernel and gaming tools preinstalled
advantages: Gaming stack ready out of the box
disadvantages: Heavier RAM use than plain Arch

name: Solus
summary: Independent, curated rolling desktop. Simple and self-contained.
disadvantages: Small project: check current release and support information

name: Arch Linux
summary: Build-it-yourself rolling distro. You choose every piece.
disadvantages: Things can break if you skip the news
Time cost to set up well
requirements: 2 GB disk minimum, 20 GB+ for desktop use

name: Gentoo
summary: Source-based distro compiled for your exact machine.
advantages: Fine control over build options and system features
Learn Linux deeply by building it

name: Void Linux
summary: Independent, fast, systemd-free. Uses runit and xbps.
advantages: Very fast boot and low overhead
disadvantages: Smaller repos than Arch or Debian
musl variant breaks some proprietary apps
requirements: 2 GB disk minimum, more for a desktop

name: NixOS
summary: Declarative Linux: your whole system defined in one config file.
advantages: Broken update? Boot the previous one
disadvantages: New language and concepts to learn
Some software needs extra packaging work

name: Slackware
summary: The oldest surviving distro. Unix-like, minimal magic.
advantages: Extremely stable and simple under the hood

name: Alpine Linux
summary: Tiny, security-focused distro built on musl and busybox.
requirements: 128 MB RAM for base, more for desktop
Around 130 MB disk for minimal install

name: antiX
summary: systemd-free Debian for very old or very small hardware.
specs: IceWM and other light window managers
Runs live from USB with persistence

name: Qubes OS
summary: Security by isolation: every app runs in its own virtual machine.
advantages: Separate qubes help limit the effect of a compromised app
disadvantages: Gaming and GPU work basically no
requirements: 64-bit Intel/AMD with VT-x + EPT or AMD-V + RVI

name: Kali Linux
summary: The standard penetration-testing toolkit. Not a daily driver.
disadvantages: Not meant as a main desktop OS
Root-first habits are bad for daily use

name: Tails
summary: Live OS designed for privacy, with Tor networking and optional encrypted storage.
advantages: Amnesic design, with optional persistent storage

name: Windows 11 Enterprise LTSC / IoT LTSC
summary: Microsoft's own minimal Windows: fewer apps, long support, no yearly feature churn.
specs: No preinstalled consumer apps or Store games
New features only via the next LTSC release
advantages: Official and fully supported by Microsoft
Very stable for kiosks and work PCs
disadvantages: Sold through volume/IoT licensing, not retail
Microsoft Store not included by default
Stays on its feature set for years
requirements: Same as Windows 11: TPM 2.0, Secure Boot capable

name: Windows 11 SE
summary: Microsoft's locked-down, cloud-first edition for school laptops.
requirements: 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage class devices
Managed by a school IT account

name: Windows S mode (10 / 11)
summary: Normal Windows restricted to Microsoft Store apps and Edge. A switch, not a separate ISO.
specs: Edge and Bing locked as defaults
One-way switch out of S mode, free
advantages: Better battery and performance on cheap PCs
disadvantages: No Chrome, Steam or classic desktop apps in S mode
requirements: Any PC that ships with S mode

name: tiny11 / tiny11builder
summary: Open script that strips a Windows 11 ISO you already own. No prebuilt ISO, no activation tricks.
specs: tiny11 Core: ultra-small, for testing VMs
Uses Microsoft's own tools (DISM) on your ISO
advantages: You build it from your own licensed ISO
Removes TPM and hardware checks for VMs
Builder output stays updateable; Core does not
disadvantages: tiny11 Core cannot add languages, updates or features
Removing components can break apps later
requirements: A genuine Windows 11 ISO and licence
PowerShell and a Windows PC to build
Resulting install needs ~8 GB RAM realistically

name: AtlasOS
summary: Open-source playbook that tunes a stock Windows install for gaming. No ISO download involved.
specs: AME Wizard playbook applied to stock Windows
advantages: You start from your own clean Windows install
disadvantages: Security settings vary by version and the choices made during setup
Some Windows features and apps stop working
Unofficial: Microsoft support will not help

name: ReviOS
summary: Privacy and performance playbook, applied to your own clean Windows install.
specs: AME Wizard playbook on stock Windows
Keeps more features working than hardcore builds
advantages: Balance of speed and everyday usability
Applied to your own licensed install
requirements: AME Wizard from the official site
Willingness to reinstall if something breaks

name: Ghost Spectre Superlite
summary: Third-party modified Windows images. For awareness, not recommendation. Piracy depends on redistribution and activation rights.
specs: Removed components and security settings vary by build
Publisher claims do not establish trust or a valid licence
advantages: May use fewer background resources; results vary and were not tested
disadvantages: Cannot verify the contents or licence of any offered image here
Unknown modifications can create security, update and compatibility risks

Publisher claims do not establish trust or a valid licence
advantages: May use fewer background resources; results vary and were not tested
disadvantages: Cannot verify the contents or licence of any offered image here
Unknown modifications can create security, update and compatibility risks
Unauthorized redistribution or activation would be piracy
